Model reference

Source: vignettes/models.Rmd
models.Rmd

This vignette states, for every model of mortensor, the model equation, the estimation method, how the forecast is generated, the defaults, and which sources of uncertainty the forecast draws contain. It is meant as the basis of a methods section. summary() of a fitted model prints the same information for the actual fit, mt_parameters() returns the estimates.

library(mortensor)
x <- mt_example(deaths = "single", years = 1995:2019)
summary(mt_fit(lee_carter(), x))
#> Lee-Carter
#>   data: 2 strata; ages 30 to 100+; periods 1995-2019
#>   model and uncertainty:
#>     log m(x,t) = a(x) + b(x) k(t), estimated by Poisson maximum likelihood
#>     (Brouhns et al. 2002). k(t) follows a random walk with drift; draws include
#>     its innovations and the uncertainty of the drift. a(x) and b(x) are fixed
#>     (parameter uncertainty with bootstrapped()). Predictive draws add Poisson
#>     variation of the deaths given the rates. Jump-off: fitted rates.
#>   fit: Poisson deviance 3371.3 on 3550 cells (0.95 per cell); 3.9% of deviance residuals beyond +/-2

Notation: m(x,t,i) is the central death rate at age x in year t in stratum i (deaths divided by exposure), D deaths, E exposures.

Data steps that affect every model

Step What mortensor does Function
Exposures mid-year population, or the mean of the populations at the start and the end of the year (1 January or 31 December counts; Preston, Heuveline and Guillot 2001) mt_as_exposure(type = )
Suppressed cells raking (iterative proportional fitting; Deming and Stephan 1940) of the missing counts to published totals, within optional bounds; cells that no published total covers get the mean of a Poisson distribution truncated to the bounds mt_fill_suppressed()
Unknown ages distributed over the age groups of the same stratum and year in proportion to the known deaths mt_data()
Ungrouping penalised composite link model with exposures (Rizzi, Gampe and Eilers 2015), its fitted values without rescaling to the group totals (preserve_totals = FALSE), or monotone interpolation of cumulative counts (method = "monotone"; Hyman 1983) mt_ungroup(), step_ungroup()
Smoothing over age (Poisson P-splines; Whittaker; GAM), over time (Whittaker) or the age-period surface (P-splines, Currie, Durban and Eilers 2004; quasi-Poisson te(age, year) GAM, Wood 2017); age 0 is not smoothed; models are fitted to the smoothed rates, their residuals and backtest scales come from the raw rates, and their predictive draws add Poisson deaths to the forecast rates (also for models of observed rates); smoothing over time narrows the intervals of models with a period index (check coverage, recalibrated()) mt_smooth(), step_smooth(), mt_smooth_check()
Zero deaths models on log rates use 0.5 deaths in a cell without deaths

All preprocessing steps given as prep are refitted on every training window of a backtest.

Single-population models

Lee-Carter: lee_carter()

log m(x,t) = a(x) + b(x) k(t), with sum b(x) = 1 and sum k(t) = 0 (Lee and Carter 1992).

  • Estimation: Poisson maximum likelihood (default; Brouhns, Denuit and Vermunt 2002) or SVD of the log rates (method = "svd", as demography::lca()), with k(t) re-estimated to match the observed total deaths (adjust = "dt"), the deaths by age ("dxt", Booth, Maindonald and Smith 2002) or life expectancy ("e0", Lee and Miller 2001). choose_period = TRUE fits the model to the longest recent period over which k(t) was close to linear (Booth, Maindonald and Smith 2002). Age groups without any death get a constant rate of 0.5 deaths over the training period and b(x) = 0. When the Poisson likelihood has no finite maximum (very sparse counts), b(x) is shrunk towards equal shares by a ridge penalty, and if that fails too the SVD estimates are used. These are safeguards of this package and are reported as warnings.
  • Forecast: k(t) follows a random walk with drift; the drift and the innovation variance are estimated from the year-to-year changes of k(t).
  • Jump-off: fitted rates of the last year (default) or observed rates (jump_off = "observed"; Lee and Miller 2001).
  • Uncertainty in the draws: innovations of k(t) and the uncertainty of its drift. a(x) and b(x) are fixed; bootstrap = TRUE (Poisson resamples of the fitted deaths; Renshaw and Haberman 2008) or bootstrapped() adds their uncertainty. Predictive draws add Poisson variation of the deaths given the rates, the observation model of the Poisson Lee-Carter model (Brouhns, Denuit and Vermunt 2002).
  • Rotation (rotate = TRUE; Li, Lee and Gerland 2013): as life expectancy at birth rises from e0_start (80) to e0_end (102), the age pattern of decline moves from b(x) to an ultimate pattern with equal decline below 65 (the mean of b over ages 15-64) and the shape of b(x) above. The weight follows a sine curve with power 0.5. In each path and year the index is solved again so that life expectancy at birth stays that of the unrotated forecast; rotation therefore changes the age pattern of the forecast only. In MortCast (Sevcikova et al. 2016) the path of life expectancy comes from a separate model; here it is that of the Lee-Carter draws. Rotation needs ages from 0 and computes life tables for every path and year, which is about 20 times slower.

Compositional data model: coda()

clr(d(x,t) / a(x)) = b(x) k(t) (Oeppen 2008; Bergeron-Boucher et al. 2017), where d(x,t) are the life-table deaths (radix 1), a(x) their closed geometric mean over the years and clr the centred log-ratio transformation. The model forecasts the distribution of deaths by age, so the forecast deaths always form a life table.

  • Estimation: first component of the SVD of the centred log-ratios, as model.Oeppen() of the R package MortalityForecast 0.8.1 (Pascariu), whose fitted values and point forecasts it reproduces. Life-table deaths do not determine the death rate of the open age interval, and the reference implementation forecasts the deaths only; here the log rate of the open interval is regressed on k(t).
  • Forecast: k(t) random walk with drift; deaths are transformed back to rates through the life table.
  • Jump-off: observed deaths of the last year, changed by the model (default), or fitted deaths (jump_off = "fitted").
  • Coherent version (coherent = TRUE or common_by): clr(d(x,t,i) / a(x,i)) = B(x) K(t) + b(x,i) k(t,i), with the common component from the average distribution of deaths of the strata; K(t) random walk with drift, k(t,i) AR(1) processes with mean, so strata stay close to the common trend (model.OeppenC()).
  • Uncertainty: innovations and drift of k(t) (and K(t)), innovations of the AR(1) processes. a and b are fixed. Predictive draws add Poisson variation of the deaths given the rates. All ages have equal weight on the clr scale, so the noise of ages with few deaths enters k(t): intervals can be wider than those of Lee-Carter.

Random walk with drift: rwd()

Each age: log m(x,t) = log m(x,t-1) + mu(x) + e(x,t).

  • Estimation: drift as the mean year-to-year change (over the last drift_window years); innovations are resampled vectors of observed changes across ages (innovations = "bootstrap", keeps the correlation between ages) or normal ("gaussian").
  • Uncertainty: innovations and drift. The observed changes contain the Poisson noise of two years, so the intervals are wide where deaths are few, and over long horizons very wide. The draws describe observed rates, so predictive draws add nothing.

The random walk with drift observed with noise (local level model with drift; Harvey 1989) is arima_series(order = c(0, 1, 1), drift = TRUE), its reduced form, below. rwd(observation_noise = TRUE), a moment estimator of this package for the same model, is deprecated.

Functional demographic model: hyndman_ullah()

Calls demography::fdm() (Hyndman and Ullah 2007): the rates of each year are smoothed over age with demography::smooth.demogdata() (smooth = TRUE; settings in smooth_args), and the log rates are decomposed into a mean function and functional principal components, whose scores are forecast with time-series models. The number of components and the smoothing settings can be chosen by forecast accuracy with tuned(). Draws are simulated from the fitted model. Its intervals are those of the simulated paths, which are somewhat narrower at short horizons than demography’s analytic intervals (see the comparison vignette). Predictive draws add Poisson variation of the deaths given the rates. Without smoothing, the resampled model errors already contain the observation noise, which predictive draws then add a second time.

Time series per age: arima_series(), ets_series()

Benchmarks that model the observed log rate of every age as a separate time series with the forecast package (Hyndman and Khandakar 2008): an ARIMA model chosen by forecast::auto.arima() (drift allowed) or given by order, or an exponential smoothing model chosen by forecast::ets() (damped trends allowed). arima_series(order = c(0, 1, 1), drift = TRUE) is the local level model with drift (a random walk with drift observed with noise; Harvey 1989) in its reduced form, fitted by maximum likelihood: where deaths are few, it separates the noise of the observed rates from the trend, which the plain random walk accumulates. Uncertainty: simulated future paths of the fitted models, so the intervals grow with the horizon; ages are simulated independently and parameter uncertainty is not included. The series are observed rates, so their draws already contain observation noise.

StMoMo models: stmomo()

Calls StMoMo::fit() and simulate() (Villegas, Kaishev and Millossovich 2018) for the Lee-Carter, CBD, APC, RH, M6, M7 and M8 families. M7 adds a quadratic age term and a cohort effect to CBD; M8 a cohort effect that falls with age to zero at age xc (Cairns et al. 2009). "rh" is StMoMo’s Renshaw-Haberman model with a cohort effect without age modulation (cohortAgeFun = "1", the default of StMoMo’s rh()). The cohort effects follow an ARIMA model (gc_order; by default ARIMA(2,0,0) with a mean for M7, as in the StMoMo vignette, and ARIMA(1,1,0) with drift for the other models). For the models with a logit link, initial exposures are approximated as central exposures plus half the deaths. Draws contain the period and cohort index uncertainty that StMoMo simulates; parameter uncertainty is not included. Predictive draws add Poisson variation of the deaths given the rates.

Bayesian StMoMo models: stanmomo()

The same families (Lee-Carter, RH, APC, CBD, M6) fitted with Stan by StanMoMo (Barigou et al. 2023), with a Poisson or negative binomial likelihood. Period indexes are random walks with drift (CBD and M6: correlated), cohort effects AR(2) processes.

  • Forecast: StanMoMo forecasts inside the fit, up to h_max years.
  • Uncertainty: posterior draws of all parameters and of the future indexes. Predictive draws are draws of the posterior predictive distribution of the deaths: Poisson given the rates of each posterior draw, or, with family = "nb", negative binomial with the dispersion of the same draw (Delwarde, Denuit and Partrat 2007).
  • Convergence: the fit warns when the largest R-hat exceeds 1.05 or transitions diverged; models with cohort effects need longer chains.

Bayesian age-period-cohort model: apc_bayes()

Calls bamp::bamp() (Schmid and Held 2007): logit death probability = age + period + cohort effects with random-walk priors of order 1 or 2, binomial likelihood, MCMC. Convergence is checked with the Gelman-Rubin statistic of the identified quantities (reported by mt_parameters() as rhat); chains that have not converged are refitted with longer runs. Uncertainty: posterior samples of the forecast rates, including the uncertainty of the parameters and of the random walks of period and cohort effects; predictive draws add Poisson variation of the deaths given the rates of each draw (bamp’s binomial likelihood and overdispersion term are not carried into them). Each stratum is fitted separately, by default where the deaths were observed (5-year age groups with annual periods use periods_per_agegroup = 5; Knorr-Held and Rainer 2001). apc_select() compares random-walk orders by the deviance information criterion (Spiegelhalter et al. 2002).

Models for several populations

Li-Lee: li_lee()

log m(x,t,i) = a(x,i) + B(x) K(t) + b(x,i) k(t,i) (Li and Lee 2005).

  • Estimation: the common factor B(x) K(t) is a Lee-Carter model (SVD, k refitted to deaths) of the pooled deaths and exposures of the strata in a group (common_by, for example one common factor per sex); the stratum factors come from an SVD of the residual log rates.
  • Forecast: K(t) random walk with drift; each k(t,i) an AR(1) process, so the deviations of a stratum from the common trend stay bounded (“coherent” in the sense that the strata do not diverge). Two choices of this package differ from Li and Lee (2005), whose AR(1) processes have a constant: the AR(1) processes have no intercept, so the stratum indexes revert to zero, and their coefficient is bounded to |phi| <= 0.99 (a safeguard against unit roots, with a warning where the bound binds).
  • Jump-off: fitted rates of the last year (default), or the forecasts multiplied by the ratio of observed to fitted rates of the last year (jump_off = "observed"; Lee and Miller 2001).
  • Uncertainty: innovations and drift of K(t), innovations of the AR(1) processes (independent across strata). a, b, B and phi are fixed. Predictive draws add Poisson variation of the deaths given the rates.

Product-ratio: coherent_fdm()

The product-ratio method (Hyndman, Booth and Yasmeen 2013) models the geometric mean of the strata (the product, which carries the common trend) and the ratio of each stratum to it. coherent_fdm() is the original method with the functional data models of demography:

  • Estimation: the rates of each stratum are smoothed over age; the product and the ratios are decomposed into principal components (demography::fdm()). With common_by, each group has its own product; in a hierarchy only the bottom strata enter the product.
  • Forecast: the scores of the product follow ARIMA models, those of the ratios stationary ARFIMA models, so the ratios return towards their recent level and the strata do not diverge.
  • Uncertainty: simulated scores and resampled model errors of the product and of each ratio; the ratios of each path are rescaled to multiply to one, as in demography::forecast.fdmpr(). Predictive draws add Poisson variation of the deaths given the rates.

product_ratio(), a Lee-Carter version of the method without a published source, is deprecated in favour of coherent_fdm().

Three-way Lee-Carter model: tucker3() (experimental)

tucker3() is the three-way extension of the Lee-Carter model of Russolillo, Giordano and Haberman (2011): the mean log rate over the years of each age and stratum is removed, and the centred array of log rates [age, period, stratum] is decomposed by a Tucker3 decomposition into age, period and stratum factors linked by a core array. The estimation by higher-order orthogonal iteration (De Lathauwer, De Moor and Vandewalle 2000), the forecast of the period factors (a multivariate random walk with drift, or ARIMA/ETS models) and the ranks (default c(3, 3, 2), or chosen by an information criterion) are choices of this package. Draws carry the uncertainty of the forecast period factors; the other factors are fixed, and predictive draws add Poisson variation of the deaths given the rates. The in-sample residual variation is added only with residual_noise = TRUE, which counts the observation noise twice. transform = "coda" is deprecated (use coda()). The model is experimental: compare it with established models such as li_lee() in a backtest before using it.

Causes of death

coda_causes() (experimental) is the multiple-decrement form of coda() that Oeppen (2008) proposed for causes of death: the deaths of a multiple-decrement life table by age and cause form one composition with one index k(t), so the causes add up to all causes in every draw. Predictive draws split Poisson all-cause deaths multinomially between the causes. Only the abstract of Oeppen (2008) is published, so the implementation follows its natural reading; in a backtest on simulated causes it was less accurate than the deprecated cause_shares(). The alternative is separate models per cause made coherent with the all-cause forecast by reconciled() (below). cause_shares(), a Tucker model of cause shares without a published source, is deprecated.

Jump-off: anchored()

Forecasts start from the fitted rates of the last year for most models. anchored() moves the start of any model to the observed level: by default the forecast draws are multiplied, per age and stratum, by the ratio of observed to fitted deaths in the last training year, in every forecast year. This is the jump-off adjustment of Lee and Miller (2001), the same as lee_carter(jump_off = "observed"). Starting from the observed rates of one year carries their random variation into every forecast year, which matters where deaths are few. The other settings are package-specific options: the offset of the last years years, shrunk towards the stratum mean where deaths are few (shrink = TRUE, empirical Bayes with the moment estimator of DerSimonian and Laird 1986), and a linear fade over decay years. mt_jump_off() reports the step between the last observed (and fitted) year and the first forecast year.

Combining models

Ensembles: ensemble()

A mixture (linear pool; Gneiting and Ranjan 2013) of the predictive distributions of its components: each draw comes from one component, for all strata at once, chosen with probabilities equal to the weights. The weights are equal by default. weights = "stack" takes the weights that minimise the squared error of the weighted mean of the components’ median forecasts in an inner backtest (stacking; Breiman 1996; for mortality, Kessy et al. 2022); using them as mixture probabilities is a deviation, since they are optimal for the combination of the medians. weights = "crps" (weights inverse to the mean CRPS of an inner backtest) and top_k are package-specific. The mixture contains the uncertainty of each component and the disagreement between them.

Different models for groups of strata: stratified()

One model per level of a stratum variable, for example Lee-Carter for all-cause mortality and Li-Lee for the causes of death. The groups are fitted and forecast separately and their draws combined; inside reconciled() they can be made coherent, for example with the causes scaled to the all-cause forecast.

Reconciled forecasts: reconciled()

Forecasts of all nodes of a hierarchy (bottom strata and their totals) are made to add up draw by draw: bottom-up sums, or projections of the base forecasts with weights from their variances (WLS; Hyndman, Lee and Wang 2016), the shrunk covariance (MinT; Wickramasuriya, Athanasopoulos and Hyndman 2019), the structure (structural scaling; Athanasopoulos et al. 2017) or equal weights (OLS; Hyndman et al. 2011). The variances and covariances of WLS and MinT are those of the base forecast draws in each age and forecast year; the papers use the in-sample residuals of the base models. fixed nodes (a trusted total) are kept, as in the reconciliation with immutable forecasts of Zhang et al. (2023), approximated by a near-zero variance. Parts that a projection would make negative are held at zero and the rest projected again, a heuristic of this package that approximates the non-negative reconciliation of Wickramasuriya, Turlach and Hyndman (2020). With fixed nodes, "proportional" instead scales their parts in proportion to their forecasts (top-down allocation; Gross and Sohl 1990; Athanasopoulos, Ahmed and Hyndman 2009). Deaths add up over every hierarchy variable; exposures add up over variables that divide the population and are shared by the levels of variables such as causes of death (additive = "rates"). The exposures of the forecast years are those of the last observed year unless projections are given. The draws are reconciled as they are (dependence = "none", default); dependence = "empirical" reorders the paths of separately fitted strata first, a package-specific method related to the Schaake shuffle (Clark et al. 2004).

Score-optimal reconciliation (method = "energy_score"; Panagiotelis et al. 2023) learns the reconciliation from the base model’s own past forecasts: the reconciled draws are S (d + G y), where y are the base draws of all nodes, and d and G (per age) minimise the energy score of forecasts from n_origins inner origins in the last years of the training data, by stochastic gradient descent from OLS, as in the package ProbReco; the estimation per age, the observation noise of the training forecasts and a rescaling of the nodes before the optimisation are details of this package. It has many parameters and few training forecasts; in the package’s backtests it was less accurate than WLS.

Calibration on recent years: recalibrated()

Refits a model at several origins in the last years (default 10) of the training data, compares its forecasts with the observed rates of that window, and rescales the spread of the draws around their median per cell by one factor for all horizons that minimises the CRPS (or the interval score of one interval), with the Poisson variation of the observed deaths (negative binomial for stanmomo(family = "nb")) as in a backtest. The closest published method is the member-by-member post-processing of ensemble forecasts (Van Schaeybroeck and Vannitsem 2015); the minimum-CRPS estimation follows Gneiting et al. (2005). Ranks within each cell are kept, so the draws remain paths. Calibration widens models that were persistently too narrow (Lee-Carter on England & Wales men: 95% coverage 0.63 to 0.85 in the backtest of “Tuning and recalibration”) and can narrow mixtures that were already wide. Package-specific options: a factor that changes with the horizon as s1 h^gamma (scale = "horizon"), a correction of the drift (bias = TRUE), separate factors for age bands (ages) and calibration of the intervals of life expectancy or the ASR (quantity), which also depend on how the ages move together; n_boot reports bootstrap intervals of the factors. Beyond the longest horizon of the window the factors stay constant. Calibration keeps the model and its settings; choosing the settings themselves is tuning (below).

Bootstrap and tuning: bootstrapped(), tuned()

bootstrapped() refits a model to Poisson resamples of the deaths (parameter uncertainty): of the fitted deaths on the grid (type = "grid", default; Renshaw and Haberman 2008), or of the observed deaths at their original resolution with the preprocessing refitted as well (type = "data"; Brouhns, Denuit and Van Keilegom 2005; refitting the preprocessing is an extension of this package). tuned() chooses settings by how well they forecast the last years of the training data only (rolling-origin evaluation, Tashman 2000; mt_tune() shows the scores): model settings such as the number of components or the rank, and with spec_fun returning list(spec = , prep = ) preprocessing settings such as the smoothing parameter or the fitting window. inner_origins = 1, inner_h = 10 is the hold-out of the last ten years often used with demography::fdm(); several origins make the choice depend less on one period. The criterion can be the CRPS, the interval score or point accuracy (metric = "rmse") of rates, life expectancy or ASR (target); select = "one_se" takes the simplest setting within one standard error of the best (Hastie, Tibshirani and Friedman 2009), and by tunes groups of strata separately. The fitting period matters for Lee-Carter forecasts when the pace of decline changed (Booth, Maindonald and Smith 2002); step_window(years) makes it a preprocessing step that tuning compares across windows.

Sources of uncertainty at a glance

Model Index innovations Drift Parameters Observation noise
lee_carter() yes yes with bootstrap = TRUE Poisson, predictive draws
rwd() yes (observed changes) yes no contained in the changes
arima_series(), ets_series() yes as the fitted model no contained in the series
li_lee() yes (common and stratum) common factor no Poisson, predictive draws
coherent_fdm() yes (product and ratios) as fdm (product) no Poisson, predictive draws
tucker3() yes (period factors) yes no Poisson, predictive draws (with residual_noise = TRUE also the residual variation)
coda(), coda_causes() yes yes no Poisson, predictive draws
hyndman_ullah() yes as fdm no Poisson, predictive draws
stmomo() yes yes no Poisson, predictive draws
stanmomo() yes posterior yes (posterior) Poisson or negative binomial (posterior predictive), predictive draws
apc_bayes() yes posterior yes (posterior) Poisson, predictive draws
ensemble() of the components of the components of the components, plus model choice of the components
stratified() of the model of each group of the model of each group of the model of each group as the models
bootstrapped() of the base model of the base model yes as the base model
reconciled() of the base model, projected of the bottom strata, summed
recalibrated() of the base model, rescaled rescaled (optional correction) as the base model
anchored() of the base model of the base model as the base model

The deprecated rwd(observation_noise = TRUE), product_ratio() and cause_shares() are left out.

Predictive draws (predictive = TRUE, always used in backtests) describe observable rates. For models of expected rates they are deaths drawn given the rates of each draw and the exposures, divided by the exposures: Poisson, the observation model of the Poisson Lee-Carter model (Brouhns, Denuit and Vermunt 2002), or negative binomial with the dispersion of the posterior draw for stanmomo(family = "nb"). No other observation noise is added. For models of observed rates (rwd(), arima_series(), ets_series()) the draws already describe observable rates and nothing is added, unless the model was fitted to smoothed rates (step_smooth()): then predictive draws add Poisson deaths as well. Forecast draws of models of expected rates without predictive describe the expected rates. If intervals are too narrow on real data, that is a property of the model; recalibrated(), ensemble() and overdispersed models such as stanmomo(family = "nb") widen them.

Evaluation

mt_backtest() refits preprocessing and model at each origin and scores predictive draws against the observed log rates of the test years with the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS; Gneiting and Raftery 2007), the weighted interval score (Bracher et al. 2021), interval coverage, the probability integral transform and the absolute error of the median. Cells with estimated (suppressed) deaths are not scored unless score_estimated = TRUE. mt_dm_test() tests differences in accuracy between two models of the same backtest with the Diebold-Mariano test (Diebold and Mariano 1995): by default with the equal-weighted cosine estimate of the long-run variance and fixed-smoothing critical values from a t distribution (Lazarus et al. 2018; Coroneo and Iacone 2020), whose size is nearly correct with few overlapping origins, at the cost of low power; varestimator = "acf" gives the version of forecast::dm.test() with the correction of Harvey, Leybourne and Newbold (1997).
